text: This is Hypocenter, an on-call agent whose reasoning lives in a FalkorDB graph. When production breaks, it answers three questions: what broke, why, and will the fix work?

Start with a real failure. This is Online Boutique, from the public RCAEval benchmark, with a CPU fault injected into one service. Six services are alerting. Hypocenter walks the call graph down from the storefront, finds that currencyservice alerted first, that the alerts climb back up the path in order, and that nothing was deployed. Its answer: an infrastructure failure on currencyservice. That is the benchmark's answer too.

It runs on all three hundred and sixty RCAEval failures, in three systems, against the benchmark's own baseline code. It names the right service first in eighty one percent. On the ninety Train Ticket cases we kept out of development it scores seventy one percent, and NSigma does better. The results page says so.

Kestrel is a demo company built to show every kind of answer. Mobile logins are failing, and seven services are alerting. Four agents take the incident: triage, an investigator, a skeptic and a responder. They never pass anything to each other in code. Each one writes its handoff to the graph, and the next one reads it back.

Replay shows the run, step by step, lighting each service as it is reached. The investigator splits the alerts into three separate problems with WCC, and a minimum spanning forest shows how each one spread. The auth deploy explains the logins. The other two problems belong to other incidents.

Every suspect becomes a hypothesis, with evidence for and against it, stored as nodes. The alerts are linked into a causal chain, so why did this alert fire is a single query. And every claim in the verdict is checked against the graph.
Before anyone approves a fix, Hypocenter tries it on a copy of the graph, and says which alerts it will clear and which it leaves. A person approves. Then it checks that the alerts really cleared.

The organisers asked for two tests. Ask the same question at depth one: the judge confidently blames payments, which is only a victim. From two hops down, it finds the pool change underneath. And ask about something that is not in the graph: it says it is not modelled, not that it is safe.

The graph is also the company's memory. Ask why the pool change was made, and the answer comes from the team's chat: the proposal, the approval, and a warning about a past incident. Follow up with, who owns it, and the conversation, kept in the graph, knows what it means.
Break it changes the graph on purpose and shows how the verdict moves, each experiment on a copy that is thrown away.
All eight of FalkorDB's graph algorithms do work in an investigation, and one command, make judge-check, rebuilds and checks everything from a fresh clone. Hypocenter.
